newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French GAN could end up at heart of bid battle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French GAN could end up at heart of bid battle.

text.p: French state-controlled insurer GAN could end up at the centre of a lively bidding battle after European Commission clearance on Wednesday of a 20-billion-franc ($3.2 billion) government rescue package.
Several heavyweight European insurers including German Allianz, Belgo-Dutch firm Fortis and France's AGF have all said they are interested in GAN and several others are also waiting in the wings.

Industry analysts said the GAN sale was likely to draw intense interest given that the decks had been cleared by the Commission and that the insurer offered one of the only ways open for companies to enter or expand in France.
The rescue involves a capital injection of 11 billion and around nine billion more to cover property business divestments.
"There's going to be quite a fight for this one," said Derek Elias, London-based insurance analyst for France's Paribas.

Other analysts said it was difficult to put a price on the group before it was known how many shares would have to be issued to the state when it provided the planned capital increase of 11 billion francs, but the minimum estimate is 8.5 billion francs.
Others said it could be double that figure and more but that GAN's accounts were hard to evaluate and more time would be needed before the conditions or the sale were better known.

France's new Socialist-led government said after the green light from the Commission that it would now proceed with privatising both GAN and its profitable bank subsidiary Credit Industriel et Commercial (CIC) taking into account the interests of the firms and the state's finances.

It is one of the few privatisations to which the new government has committed itself fully since coming to power in early June, but the ministry has yet to reveal how it plans to conduct the sell-offs.
GAN made losses of 35 billion francs between 1992 and 1996, mainly because of extremely damaging investments in a property market which collapsed at the end of the 1990s.

Salomon Brothers analyst Brian Shea has estimated the value of GAM at roughtly of 8.5 billion francs and says French firm AGF, which is seen as one of the more credible contenders alongside Allianz and Fortis, could afford to pay for GAN without needing to raise fresh funds.

Several other players are known to be interested as well, including Dutch ING Groep, Italy's Assicurazioni Generali SpA and Eureko, an Amsterdam-based alliance of six European financial services firms with no French presence.

Another London-based analyst said the real attraction of GAN was the core French insurance business and the growth sector of bancassurance, where GAN has a lucrative partnership with its CIC subsidiary for the sale of life assurance through CIC's regional retail bank network.

Allianz and Fortis are keen to get a stronger foothold in France while AGF is seen as needing ther acquisition to bolster its position in the wake of the megamerger of Axa and UAP, which created the world's second largest insurance group.

Shea and other analysts said the advantage for AGF would be the potential for cost cuts. But in terms of financial muscle, it was in for a tough time if Allianz and Fortis were determined to get control GAN.
The group currently has just over 57 million shares outstanding, of which 80 percent are owned by the state.
AGF itself made no official comment on Wednesday. But it has said in the past it is interested in GAN at a "reasonable" price and possibly taking 20 to 30 percent of the banking unit CIC.

The previous centre-right government abandoned a first attempt to sell CIC by trade sale last year after getting two offers from BNP and Societe Generale, the latter of which was ruled ineligible by France's Privatisation Commission.
The assumption for the moment is that the new government will carry out the privatisation of GAN and CIC separately.
The European Commission said on Wednesday that its approval had been granted in return for a promise by Paris to launch the sell-offs as soon as possible and by June 30 1998 at the latest.

It also said that the government pledges include ensuring that half of GAN's business outside France is sold off as well as the beleaguered UIC and UIS property units, which have already been put up for sale.
The group also has to divest strategic shareholding worth some 2.4 billion francs, the Commission said in a statement.
Other names cited among possible suitors for GAN include Britain's Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Group and a combination of French mutual insurer MAAF and Switzerland's Zurich Group.
